questions.q: Why does a backend use asynchronous code when it waits for a database?
questions.explain: A backend mostly waits. If it stopped everything while waiting, it could only serve one person at a time. Asynchronous code says "call me back when it is ready" and moves on.
options: Because the database only understands asynchronous requests
So it can serve other requests while it waits, instead of standing still
Because asynchronous code uses less memory than synchronous code

2. Carry on
3. The database answered

1. Ask the database
3. The database answered
2. Carry on

2. Carry on

questions.q: The timer asks for 0 ms. What does this print?
questions.explain: JavaScript runs on one thread. The timer is due right away, but it has to wait until the synchronous code has finished and let go of the thread.

questions.q: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread. What does that mean for a long while loop that keeps the thread busy for 2 seconds on a server?
questions.explain: That is blocking code. While synchronous code runs, nothing else can, so a busy loop freezes the whole server, not just one request.
options: Only the request that started the loop waits
Nothing else can run: every request and every due timer waits until the loop ends
Node.js moves the loop to another thread automatically
The loop is paused whenever a request arrives

questions.q: A server reads a file for each request. Which should it use?
questions.explain: readFileSync blocks the thread until the file is read. The non-blocking version starts the work, gives the thread back and calls you later.
options: readFile (non-blocking), so the thread is free for other requests while the file is read
A while loop that checks whether the file is ready
It makes no difference on a server

questions.q: Node.js callbacks are error-first. What does that mean?
questions.explain: The shape is (error, result) => { … }. You must check error every time, then use the result.
options: The callback is only called when there is an error
The first argument is an error (or null if all went well), and the result comes second
Errors are thrown before the callback runs
The callback must be the first argument of the function

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For id 2 the function calls back with an error first and no result. The callback checks error and returns before touching user.

questions.q: Which is not one of the problems of "callback hell"?
questions.explain: Callbacks do pass data (the result argument). Their problems are deep nesting, repeated error checks that are easy to forget, no try/catch across steps, and double calls. Promises fix these.
options: Each step pushes the code further to the right
The same error check is repeated at every level
A buggy function could call its callback twice
Callbacks cannot pass any data to the next step

questions.q: What is a Promise?
questions.explain: A function that works asynchronously returns a promise straight away. You attach what should happen once the value is there, with .then or await.
options: An object that stands for a value you will have later
A special kind of callback that runs first
A way to make code run on a second thread

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: findTask returns a promise at once, so instanceof Promise is true and "waiting" prints next. The .then function runs later, when the value is ready.

questions.q: Which list shows the three states of a promise?
questions.explain: A promise starts pending, then becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. Fulfilled and rejected together are called settled.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A promise settles only once and never changes. The first call, reject(disk full), wins; the later calls are ignored. That rule removes the "callback called twice" bug.
options:
rejected: disk full
fulfilled: too late

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The report is longer than 10 characters, so save rejects. The .then step is skipped, .catch handles it, and .finally runs at the end either way.
options:
saved: Ada: Buy milk, Call Grace
done

questions.q: In a chain a().then(b).then(c).catch(handle), which failures does .catch(handle) receive?
questions.explain: A rejection skips the following .then steps until it reaches a .catch. One .catch at the end covers the whole chain.
options: A failure in any step above it: a, b or c
None: each step needs its own .catch

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An async function always returns a promise, even when it returns a plain value. You get the value with await or .then.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: await pauses only main. The rest of the program keeps running, so "B" prints while main waits, and "C" comes after the 20 ms.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When an async function throws, its promise is rejected. await turns the rejection back into a thrown error, which jumps to catch and skips the next line.
options:
Saved: 3
Could not save: title must not be empty
Could not save: title must not be empty

Saved: 3
This line never runs

questions.q: The await is missing. What does this print? (The last line catches the error so the program does not crash.)
questions.explain: Without await, the call returns a pending promise at once and try finishes happily. The error comes later, when the try block is long gone.
options:
Saved, I think
later: title must not be empty
Could not save: title must not be empty

Could not save: title must not be empty
later: title must not be empty

questions.q: What happens in Node.js when a rejected promise is never handled (no await in a try, no .catch)?
questions.explain: An error nobody saw is dangerous, so Node.js crashes on it. Whenever you call an async function, either await it or attach a .catch.
options: It is an unhandled rejection, and Node.js stops the whole process

questions.q: You need the user count and the task count, and neither depends on the other. What is the better way?
questions.explain: Independent waits should run at the same time. Two 100 ms lookups then take about 100 ms, not 200. Use sequential awaits only when a step needs the previous result.
options: Start both, then wait for them together with Promise.all

questions.q: The slow promise finishes last. What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all keeps the results in the same order as the input, whatever order they finish in.

questions.q: You must load 10,000 records from a database. Why not start all 10,000 queries at once with Promise.all?
questions.explain: Parallel is not always right. Start a small number at a time (a batch), wait for them with Promise.all, then start the next batch.
options: The database would struggle with so much at once; for large lists, work in batches
The results would come back in random order
JavaScript would run them one after another anyway

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all rejects with the first error. The successful "tasks" value is lost. Use allSettled when partial results are useful.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: allSettled never fails. It reports each promise in input order: status plus value when fulfilled, or reason when rejected.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.race settles like whichever promise settles first, success or failure. The failure came first, so the race fails.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.any waits for the first success and skips failures. It only fails if every promise fails.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When every promise fails, Promise.any rejects with an AggregateError. Its errors array lists every reason.

questions.q: A page needs the user and may show tasks and notifications. You want every result that arrived, even if some services failed. Which should you use?
questions.explain: allSettled reports each promise separately and never fails, so you keep the partial results. all would throw away everything on the first failure.

questions.q: How does the lesson's withTimeout(promise, ms) put a time limit on a promise?
questions.explain: Promise.race([promise, timeout]) settles with whichever comes first. If the timer rejects first, the slow work counts as failed. finally then clears the timer.
options: It races the promise against a timer that rejects after ms
It uses a while loop that checks the clock

questions.q: Why does withTimeout call clearTimeout(timer) in .finally?
questions.explain: When the real work wins, the timer is no longer needed. Clearing it stops it from running later and from keeping the process alive.
options: So the timer does not keep the program waiting after the work has already finished
To restart the timer for the next request

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tasks answers in 10 ms, inside the 40 ms limit. notes needs 80 ms, so the timer rejects first and it counts as failed.

questions.q: In the dashboard loader, what happens when the user service fails, and when the notifications service fails?
questions.explain: The user is required, so the loader re-throws user.reason. Tasks and notifications are nice to have: the page shows the rest and reports what is missing.
options: Neither fails the request; both go into missing
A user failure fails the whole request; a notifications failure only goes into missing
A notifications failure fails the request; a user failure goes into missing

questions.q: In retry, the lesson writes return await fn(attempt); inside try. Why not just return fn(attempt);?
questions.explain: This is the forgotten-await bug again. await makes the rejection happen inside the try, so catch can count the attempt and try again.
options: Without await, the promise is returned before it fails, and catch never sees the error

questions.q: Finish the async function completeTask(id): wait 20 ms, find the task in db, throw new Error(`Task ${id} not found`) if it is missing, otherwise return a copy with done: true. The program should print Buy milk true and then Task 9 not found.
questions.explain: Inside an async function, a throw rejects its promise, and the caller's await turns it back into an error for catch.
questions.expected:
Buy milk true
Task 9 not found

questions.q: Write wait(ms): it returns a promise that is fulfilled after ms milliseconds, using setTimeout. The program should print start, then after 20 ms.
questions.explain: new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms)) turns a timer callback into a promise you can await.

questions.q: getUser uses an error-first callback. Write getUserAsync(id) that returns a promise: reject with the error, or fulfil with the user. The program should print Ada and then failed: user 5 not found.
questions.explain: Wrap the callback call in new Promise. The error-first check decides between reject(error) and resolve(user). Now callers can use await and try/catch.

questions.q: Finish loadCounts() so it runs countTasks() and countUsers() at the same time with Promise.all, and returns { tasks, users }. The program should print { tasks: 3, users: 2 }.
questions.explain: Call both functions first (that starts them), pass the promises to Promise.all, and destructure the array of values.

questions.q: Write retry(fn, attempts). It calls the async function fn(attempt); if that fails, it tries again, up to attempts times in total. If every attempt fails, it throws the last error. The program should print tasks loaded and then gave up: service unavailable.
questions.explain: Use return await fn(attempt) inside try, so a failure is caught and the loop tries again. After the loop, throw the last error you saw.
questions.expected:
tasks loaded
gave up: service unavailable

questions.q: Load the tasks with ids 1 to 6, but never more than 2 at a time: split the ids into batches of 2 and use Promise.all for each batch. Push the results into loaded in order. The program should print [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 ].
questions.explain: Each batch runs in parallel, and the await inside the loop makes the batches run one after another. Promise.all keeps each batch in input order.

questions.q: Finish withTimeout(promise, ms): race the promise against a timer that rejects with new Error("timed out") after ms, and clear the timer in finally. The program should print fast and then timed out.
questions.explain: Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first. The timer rejects the slow call; finally clears the timer when the fast call wins.

questions.q: Finish loadAll(sources) with Promise.allSettled. Return { values, missing }: the values of the fulfilled promises, and the error messages of the rejected ones, both in input order. The program should print [ 'tasks', 'users' ] [ 'notes down' ].
questions.explain: allSettled never rejects. Check each result's status: use value for fulfilled ones and reason.message for rejected ones.

questions.q: Finish the async function report(id) with await (no .then): get the user with getUser(id), then the tasks with getTasks(user), and return the user's name, a colon and the tasks joined with ", ". The program should print Ada: Buy milk, Call Grace.
questions.explain: Each await replaces one .then, and the code reads top to bottom. The second step needs the user, so sequential awaits are right here.
